t: No State or unit of general local government may use any amounts received pursuant to section 2301 to fund any project that seeks to use the power of eminent domain, unless eminent domain is employed only for a public use: Provided, That for purposes of this section, public use shall not be construed to include economic development that primarily benefits private entities.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that the mention of States, local governments and "public use" signals outside-party involvement. But the section only restricts how grant recipients may spend federal funds on eminent domain projects. It sets up no consultation, comment period, hearing, advisory body, rulemaking or right to sue over a federal decision.
fable.s: No State or unit of general local government may use any amounts received pursuant to section 2301 to fund any project that seeks to use the power of eminent domain

qwen_block.w: This section imposes a restriction on how state and local governments may use federal funds, specifically prohibiting the use of eminent domain for private economic development. It does not require the federal government to consult with, coordinate with, or receive input from outside parties before making a decision. The actors involved are the federal government (setting the rule) and state/local governments (complying with the rule), but there is no mechanism for public participation, advisory boards, or consultation with non-federal entities in the decision-making process described.
qwen_block.s: No State or unit of general local government may use any amounts received pursuant to section 2301 to fund any project that seeks to use the power of eminent domain, unless eminent domain is employed only for a public use: Provided, That for purposes of this section, public use shall not be construed to include economic development that primarily benefits private entities.

opus.w: This provision only limits how States and local governments that receive section 2301 funds may spend them, specifically on eminent-domain projects. It names non-federal governments, but only as funding recipients under a restriction, not as parties consulted on a federal decision. It sets up no comment period, hearing, advisory body, rulemaking, or right to sue.
opus.s: No State or unit of general local government may use any amounts received pursuant to section 2301 to fund any project that seeks to use the power of eminent domain, unless eminent domain is employed only for a public use

qwen_chat.w: This section imposes a substantive restriction on how state and local governments may use federal funds. It does not require the federal government to consult with outside parties, nor does it establish a process for public participation, advisory committees, or hearings. The interaction is purely regulatory between the federal government and state/local entities regarding fund usage, without involving the general public or other outside entities in the decision-making process.
qwen_chat.s: No State or unit of general local government may use any amounts received pursuant to section 2301 to fund any project that seeks to use the power of eminent domain, unless eminent domain is employed only for a public use
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the restriction on eminent domain implies a need for public input or legal challenges by private entities, thus involving outside parties. However, the text itself only sets a substantive legal limit on how state and local governments can use funds; it does not mandate any specific process for consultation, comment, or participation by outside parties in the decision-making process. The definition requires that the federal government consult or coordinate with outsiders, or that outsiders have a defined role in a federal decision. Here, the federal government is simply imposing a condition on grant recipients (states/local governments). There is no mechanism described for public participation, advisory boards with non-federal members, or required consultation with the public.
